# **Comprehensive Feasibility Study of KeeperHub Infrastructure: Cost Surface, Licensing, and Self-Hosting Contingency Analysis**

## **Feasibility of a Zero-Cost Hackathon Project**

An exhaustive evaluation of the KeeperHub platform confirms that a decentralized application or autonomous agent project can be successfully developed, tested, and submitted to the hackathon within the designated window of July 27 to August 13, 2026, with an absolute spend of zero dollars1. The platform is currently operating in public beta, during which all workflow executions are completely free and unmetered, requiring no credit card registration at any stage1.  
Following the conclusion of the public beta, KeeperHub's permanent Free tier transitions to a structured cap of 5,000 free executions per month1. One execution is defined as a single workflow run, whether it performs a basic smart contract read or triggers a complex, multi-step transaction on-chain1.

This mathematical derivation aligns with the platform’s documentation, which simplifies the allocation to a frequency of one workflow execution running approximately every nine minutes, 24/7, for an entire month1.  
Under the default Free tier, the platform enforces a strict hard-cap policy1. When the 5,000-execution limit is reached, active workflows are automatically paused rather than generating surprise overage fees1. Overage billing of $2.00 per 1,000 executions is restricted to paid tiers1.  
To offset on-chain transaction fees, the Free tier includes $1.00 of gas credits per month, covering gas fees across all supported EVM networks, particularly low-cost Layer 2 chains such as Base and Arbitrum1. This structural design allows developers to ship working on-chain prototypes without financial friction1.

## **Comprehensive Cost Surface and Tool-by-Tool Cost Matrix**

The table below outlines the cost surfaces, metering mechanisms, and constraints associated with individual KeeperHub tools and platform capabilities.

| Tool / Service Component | Cost Status | Metering & Fee Structure | Limits & Hard Caps |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Remote MCP Endpoint** (https://app.keeperhub.com/mcp) | Free to Call3 | No per-call meter on metadata or discovery commands (e.g., listing workflows, validating templates)1. | Workflow runs initiated via execute\_workflow consume the account's monthly execution limit1. |
| **KeeperHub CLI** (npm @keeperhub/cli or kh) | Free4 | Free to download, install, and run locally4. Built in Go with an MIT license4. | Platform interactions are bound by the credentials and limits of the connected organization account3. |
| **Account Creation & Wallet Provisioning** | Free1 | Account setup is free with no credit card required1. Generates a Turnkey MPC wallet5. | Automatically generates a single hardware-enclave organization wallet6. |
| **Private Workflows** (Within Org) | Free1 | Billed strictly against the organization's execution quota1. Logic remains private to the org7. | Unlimited during beta1; capped at 5,000 executions/month under the permanent post-beta Free tier1. |
| **Listed Workflows** (Marketplace) | Free to Publish7 | Free to deploy7. Earnings are collected from external callers via x402 or MPP7. | Subject to marketplace security curation and edit-while-listed validation policies9. |
| **Platform Seat & Project Limits** | Free1 | Feature-parity across tiers ensures no paywalls on seats, team members, or projects1. | Limited only by the aggregate execution and gas credit limits of the hosting organization1. |
| **Gas Credit Allowance** | Free ($1/mo)1 | Automatically applied to cover EVM on-chain transaction gas fees across supported chains1. | Hard-capped at $1.00 per month on the Free tier1. Unused credits expire at the end of the billing cycle. |

### **Metering and Endpoint Constraints**

The remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server located at https://app.keeperhub.com/mcp is free to configure and call for discovery-based tooling3. Standard queries such as list\_workflows, validate\_workflow, and get\_execution\_logs do not invoke the workflow execution engine, meaning they are unmetered and do not count toward monthly limits1.  
However, calling the execute\_workflow tool triggers a live operational run of the targeted workflow3. Each triggered run consumes exactly one execution from the organization's monthly quota1.  
The kh command-line interface, along with associated developer packages such as @keeperhub/sdk and framework-specific integration plugins (including @keepergate/openclaw and @ethglobal-openagent/openclaw-keeperhub), is completely free to install, configure, and execute4. These client-side tools run locally and do not impose proprietary software licensing fees4.  
All network calls routed from the CLI to the hosted KeeperHub API are authenticated via an organization-scoped API key and are limited strictly by the quota constraints of the hosting account3.

## **Operational Mechanics of Workflows: Private vs. Listed**

The operational dichotomy between a listed workflow and a private workflow centers on accessibility, computational allocation, and monetization dynamics. A private workflow is designed to execute strictly within the internal boundaries of an organization7. The computational overhead of these executions is billed directly against the organization's monthly quota1.  
Conversely, a listed workflow acts as a public-facing service deployed to the KeeperHub DeFi strategies Marketplace7. While the publisher retains absolute privacy over the internal logic and proprietary code of the workflow, external agents and protocols can discover and invoke the workflow over open programmatic interfaces like the Model Context Protocol or REST APIs7.

### **The Pay-Per-Call Economics (x402 and MPP)**

Listed workflows leverage machine payment standards to establish an autonomous, pay-per-call economic layer7. When an external system triggers a listed workflow, the interaction does not consume the creator's execution limits or gas credits1. Instead, the caller pays for the execution in USD Coin (USDC) via standard cryptographic payment channels7.  
This pay-per-call flow is governed by two complementary standards: the HTTP-native x402 protocol and the Machine Payments Protocol (MPP)8.

\[External AI Agent\] \---\> (HTTP POST /execute\_workflow) \---\> \[KeeperHub Execution Gateway\]  
                                                                    |  
                                                    (Returns HTTP 402 \+ Challenge)  
                                                                    |  
\[External AI Agent\] \<--- (WWW-Authenticate: Payment Challenge) \<----+  
        |  
 (Settle USDC via x402 on Base or MPP on Tempo)  
        |  
        v  
\[External AI Agent\] \---\> (HTTP POST with Authorization Header) \---\> \[KeeperHub Execution Gateway\]  
                                                                            |  
                                                                  (Verifies & Executes)  
                                                                            |  
\[External AI Agent\] \<--- (Returns Result \+ Payment-Receipt) \<---------------+

The execution sequence begins when an external agent initiates a request to run a workflow13. The server halts the request and returns an HTTP 402 Payment Required response containing a payment challenge13. The caller's agentic wallet parses the challenge, signs an on-chain stablecoin authorization, settles the fee, and retries the request with a payment proof13.  
Once verified on-chain, the gateway executes the workflow, shielding the creator's assets while generating direct revenue7.

### **Marketplace Pricing and Distribution**

On active agent-centric marketplaces such as RelAI, which index x402 and MPP endpoints, the price distribution for programmatic calls is centered under $0.05 for standard operations, though it spans a wider range depending on computational complexity18:

| Pricing Tier | Typical Price Range (USDC) | Target Operations | Common Examples |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Micro-transactions** | $0.001 to $0.005 | High-frequency, low-overhead data requests and read-only directory queries18. | Fetching indexer states, querying price feeds, or scanning open jobs18. |
| **Standard Operations** | $0.01 to $0.05 | Core workflow execution, web search, structured data extraction, and routing logic16. | Running transaction simulations, executing standard swaps, or retrieving APY gap metrics16. |
| **Complex Executions** | $0.05 to $1.00 | Multi-step write operations, cross-chain bridging, or generative AI actions18. | Executing cross-chain transfers, contract deployments, or generating custom AI summaries18. |

## **Legal, Licensing, and Security Evaluation**

An analysis of KeeperHub's public licensing and platform documentation indicates no restrictive clauses that would hinder hackathon development, commercial deployment, or open-source distribution:

1. **Code Ownership:** There are no provisions granting KeeperHub ownership of or intellectual property rights to your workflow logic, custom typescript scripts, or agent logic4. All workflow definitions exported using the "use workflow" directive remain under the user's sole ownership19.  
2. **Key Custody and Portability:** Platform terms enforce a non-custodial wallet model6. Cryptographic keys are stored inside Turnkey enclaves and can be exported as an encrypted bundle at any time without administrative intervention or delay6.  
3. **Hackathon Utility:** KeeperHub is actively sponsoring the event with structured cash prizes, and the evaluation criteria heavily weight real on-chain executions2. This aligns with an open developer terms framework that encourages commercial experimentation2.

### **Security Architecture and Risk Mitigation**

To limit the financial risk of autonomous operations, developers can configure programmable, multi-tiered safety hooks using the @keeperhub/wallet package4. This package integrates three-tier safety hooks that enforce strict risk-managed ceilings4.  
These configurations prevent runaway agent spending by programmatically capping daily on-chain transactions4. These safety layers ensure that even if an agent's logic loops unexpectedly, its total financial exposure is hard-capped on the client side4.

## **Technical Comparison: Hosted SaaS vs. Open-Source**

The core application engine of KeeperHub is distributed under the Apache 2.0 open-source license, while its developer tooling (such as the CLI and plugins) is released under the MIT license4. This open-source framework allows developers to self-host the application21.  
However, a comparison of the hosted SaaS product (app.keeperhub.com) against the self-hosted open-source codebase reveals critical operational differences5.

| Architectural Feature | Hosted SaaS Platform (app.keeperhub.com) | Self-Hosted Open Source Core (KeeperHub/keeperhub) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Licensing Framework** | Proprietary managed services layer layered over the open-source engine4. | Core workflow engine is Apache 2.0; CLI and plugins are MIT licensed4. |
| **Wallet Security Model** | Integrated Turnkey MPC wallets secured inside hardware enclaves (TEEs)5. | Requires manual integration and licensing of Turnkey or Para MPC developer accounts21. |
| **Infrastructure Overhead** | Zero setup. Managed multi-RPC failover, smart gas estimation, and transaction retries5. | Requires hosting and configuring PostgreSQL 16, Redis, LocalStack SQS, and execution workers21. |
| **Local Testing Mocks** | Built-in support for simulated testnets (such as Sepolia) with zero config5. | Relies on LocalStack Pro to simulate SQS. Refuses to boot without a LocalStack Pro license token21. |
| **Transaction Delivery** | SLA-backed transaction routing, incorporating private MEV protection pathways8. | Transaction delivery depends on the RPC endpoints provided in the environment file21. |

While the hosted SaaS product provides Turnkey MPC enclaves, multi-RPC failover, and smart gas estimation out of the box, self-hosting requires manual infrastructure provisioning and developer-managed wallet keys5.

## **Contingency Analysis: Self-Hosting Fallback Path**

If self-hosting is required, the deployment process demands substantial infrastructure and is subject to a critical licensing blocker21.

### **The LocalStack Pro Blocker**

The primary obstacle to self-hosting the open-source repository on standard free-tier cloud platforms (such as Render, Railway, or Fly.io) is its dependency on LocalStack Pro21. The Docker Compose environment distributed with the codebase utilizes LocalStack SQS to handle workflow execution queues21.  
The configuration files will refuse to build or boot without a valid LOCALSTACK\_AUTH\_TOKEN21. While developer tokens are available, this dependency adds configuration overhead and introduces a third-party commercial service into what would otherwise be a self-contained deployment21.

### **Infrastructure Requirements and Resource Footprint**

Running a fully operational instance of KeeperHub requires setting up a distributed microservices topology21. This architecture includes:

1. **Application Layer:** A Next.js 16 (App Router) engine running on Node.js version 22 or higher (Node 18 is not supported)21.  
2. **Database Layer:** PostgreSQL 16 managed via Drizzle ORM21.  
3. **Message Broker & Cache:** Redis (Port 6379\) alongside LocalStack SQS (Port 4566\) to orchestrate task queues21.  
4. **Workflow Orchestration Daemons:** Standalone background processes for the Scheduler, Block Dispatcher, Event Tracker, and Executor21.

The resource requirements for this multi-container stack exceed the CPU and memory limits of standard free-tier hosting services. Running Next.js 16, PostgreSQL 16, Redis, LocalStack, and multiple background daemons in a single environment will exhaust standard free-tier RAM allocations, leading to out-of-memory (OOM) failures.

### **Self-Hosted Execution Modes**

The platform can be configured using the EXECUTION\_MODE environment variable, which alters its runtime dependencies21:

* isolated (Default): Spuns up isolated Kubernetes Job containers via Docker, kubectl, and minikube for every workflow run21. This mode is highly resource-intensive and cannot run on standard lightweight PaaS providers21.  
* complex: Executes Web3 write actions in Kubernetes Jobs and handles read-only steps in-process21.  
* process: Runs all workflow executions in-process within the main Node application21. While this mode bypasses the need for Kubernetes, it still requires PostgreSQL, Redis, and a LocalStack Pro SQS queue21.

### **Deployment Reference Configuration**

To deploy the platform locally or on a private virtual private server (VPS), the following environment variables must be defined21:

Code snippet  
\# Database Credentials (Strictly read by drizzle-kit from .env)  
DATABASE\_URL=postgresql://user:password@localhost:5433/keeperhub

\# Authentication Setup  
BETTER\_AUTH\_SECRET=a\_highly\_secure\_random\_string\_here  
BETTER\_AUTH\_URL=http://localhost:3000

\# Infrastructure Queue Gateway  
LOCALSTACK\_AUTH\_TOKEN=your\_localstack\_pro\_token\_here

\# Runtime Configuration  
EXECUTION\_MODE=process

Prior to running the initialization routines, the external Docker volumes and virtual network interfaces must be manually configured in the host environment21:

Bash  
\# Set up Docker virtual networking mesh  
docker network create keeperhub-network

\# Allocate persistent volumes for storage engines  
docker volume create keeperhub\_db\_data  
docker volume create keeperhub\_node\_modules  
docker volume create keeperhub\_localstack\_data

\# Execute the database seed and setup sequences  
make dev-setup

## **Conclusions and Strategic Recommendations**

The hosted KeeperHub SaaS SKU (app.keeperhub.com) offers a viable zero-cost environment for the hackathon1. The public beta provides unlimited, unmetered executions with no credit card requirement1. This hosted solution eliminates the complex infrastructure setup, licensing, and database management required by the open-source repository5.  
Additionally, the hosted platform provides built-in Turnkey MPC wallet security, eliminating the need to manage private keys on client servers5.  
In contrast, the self-hosting path is not feasible on a $0 budget due to its strict dependency on a paid LocalStack Pro license token21. Running the full microservices stack—including Next.js, Postgres, Redis, LocalStack, and background daemons—also exceeds the resource limits of standard free cloud hosting tiers21.  
Therefore, the recommended strategy is to deploy the hackathon application directly on the hosted SaaS platform5. This path guarantees $0 in development costs, provides robust wallet security, and ensures full compatibility with the hackathon's on-chain execution criteria1.
